props.title: Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
props.initialSlug: Man's dark alter ego wreaks terror in London

sections.content: John Barrymore's transformative performance in Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde (1920) revolutionized horror cinema's approach to physical metamorphosis. Without relying on elaborate makeup or special effects, Barrymore contorted his face and body to create Hyde's monstrous appearance, influencing decades of horror actors. This technique directly inspired Lon Chaney's work in The Phantom of the Opera (1925) and laid groundwork for future Jekyll/Hyde adaptations like Fredric March's Oscar-winning turn in Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde and Spencer Tracy's version in Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde.

sections.content: Director John S. Robertson's atmospheric approach to Victorian London created a template for Gothic horror settings that influenced films like London After Midnight (1927) and Dracula (1931). The film's innovative use of tinting and early special effects during Jekyll's transformation scenes demonstrated silent cinema's ability to convey psychological horror through purely visual means, a technique later perfected in The Man Who Laughs (1928).

The film's exploration of duality and repression resonated deeply in post-WWI society, making it one of the first horror films to tackle sophisticated psychological themes. This approach influenced later works like M (1931) and Mad Love (1935), which similarly explored the darkness lurking beneath respectable surfaces. The movie's success also helped establish Paramount Pictures as a major player in horror cinema, leading to their subsequent supernatural thrillers of the 1920s. sections.content: The film's groundbreaking practical effects and makeup techniques, achieved through camera tricks and Barrymore's physical performance, established a new standard for horror transformation sequences. This influence can be traced through Werewolf of London (1935), The Wolf Man (1941), and even modern practical effects masterpieces like An American Werewolf in London (1981). The film's psychological complexity also helped legitimize horror as a vehicle for serious artistic expression.
